The defendant, Jake Williams, 31, a retail store manager, is charged with assault after a fight outside a sports bar at about 11:40 p.m. The complainant suffered a broken nose and needed six stitches above the left eye.

A security camera above the bar entrance shows Jake striking the complainant twice in the face. The camera does not cover the two or three seconds before the first punch, because both people stepped partly out of frame. The bouncer testified that the two had argued inside over a spilled drink and that Jake "looked angry" on the way out. The complainant testified to being punched without warning while walking to a car.

Jake testified that the complainant followed him outside, shouted threats, and shoved him hard against a parked car, and that he punched only to get free. A bartender confirmed that the complainant left the bar right after Jake, but did not see what happened outside. Responding officers noted a scrape on Jake's elbow. The complainant's blood alcohol level was 0.14; Jake's was 0.06.

The prosecution argues that two punches to the face, including one after the complainant had stepped back, go beyond what self-defense allows. The defense argues that the video starts too late to show who began the fight.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 26, a bank loan officer, is charged with assault for a beating at a bus stop at around 10:15 p.m. The complainant suffered a fractured wrist and bruised ribs and could not describe the attacker, who wore a dark jacket with the hood up.

A food truck worker about 15 meters away watched the attack under a streetlight. Four days later, the worker picked Jake out of a six-photo lineup and told the detective, "I'm pretty sure, maybe 80 percent." The attacker took the complainant's phone, and that phone connected to a cell tower near Jake's apartment about 40 minutes after the attack. Police found no stolen property and no dark jacket during a search of the apartment.

Jake testified that he was at home all evening. Phone records show him sending text messages from home at 9:58 p.m. and 10:31 p.m.; the bus stop is about a 12-minute drive away. His roommate testified that Jake was home but admitted to falling asleep at around 10:00 p.m.

The prosecution argues that the eyewitness identification and the phone's location point to the defendant. The defense argues that the identification is uncertain and that the tower covers several thousand residents.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 38, a city bus driver, is charged with assault after a confrontation in a convenience store parking lot. The complainant suffered a concussion and a cut on the scalp that required staples.

Jake admits pushing the complainant, who fell and hit the curb. He testified that the two had a short argument about a parking space, and that the complainant then grabbed a glass bottle from a trash bin and swung it at his head. Jake said he pushed the complainant away to avoid being hit.

No bottle was recovered. The store clerk saw the push through the window but did not see the moments before it. The clerk testified that the complainant "had something in one hand" but could not say what it was. The complainant denied picking up anything and said Jake came at them "out of nowhere." Officers found broken glass in the lot, but the store manager testified that broken glass was common there.

Jake called 911 right after the fall and stayed at the scene until police arrived. The complainant has one prior conviction for disorderly conduct.

The prosecution argues that the push was disproportionate and that the bottle story was invented. The defense argues that the defendant reacted to a weapon and immediately sought help.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 29, a line cook, is charged with assault after a fight in the kitchen of the restaurant where he worked. The complainant, a coworker, suffered a deep bruise on the forearm and a sprained shoulder.

The complainant testified that Ryan became angry over an order mix-up and struck them with a metal ladle. A dishwasher, who is a close friend of the complainant, supported that version. A second cook, who carpools with Ryan, testified that the complainant grabbed Ryan's collar first and that Ryan raised the ladle only to block.

The emergency physician testified that the forearm bruise could come either from a blow or from a defensive block against a held object. The kitchen camera was broken that week. The restaurant manager testified that both employees had received written warnings for arguments during shifts in the previous month.

Text messages show that Ryan wrote to a friend that night: "I lost it at work, I messed up." Ryan testified that the message referred to yelling during the argument, not to hitting anyone.

The prosecution argues that the injuries and the defendant's own message show an intentional attack. The defense argues that the evidence is balanced and that the defendant acted defensively.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 34, an insurance claims adjuster, is charged with assault after a neighbor was found injured in the shared driveway of a duplex at about 7:00 p.m. The complainant suffered a fractured cheekbone and could not identify the attacker, saying they were struck from behind.

Material under the complainant's fingernails contained Brett's DNA. The two had a long-running dispute about parking, and a third neighbor recorded a phone video at about 1:00 p.m. that day showing the two pushing and grabbing each other for about ten seconds before separating. No one was injured in that first incident.

Brett testified that he left for a client inspection at 3:00 p.m. and returned after 8:00 p.m. The client confirmed that Brett was at the inspection site until about 6:15 p.m. The drive back takes about 35 minutes. No one saw Brett between 6:15 p.m. and 8:00 p.m. A wooden board with traces of the complainant's blood was found by the driveway, but no usable fingerprints were found on it.

The prosecution argues that the DNA, the motive, and the window of opportunity point to the defendant. The defense argues that the DNA is explained by the recorded midday scuffle and that nothing places the defendant at the scene at 7:00 p.m.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 27, a hotel front desk clerk, is charged with assault after punching a stranger at a late-night food stand. The complainant lost a tooth and suffered a cut lip.

Ryan admits throwing one punch. He testified that the complainant was standing very close to his friend, yelling, and had pulled back a fist, and that he struck first to stop what he believed was an imminent attack on the friend. The friend testified to the same account.

The complainant testified to complaining about the friend cutting in line, and said there was no raised fist and no threat. The vendor at the stand testified that the complainant was "loud and in the friend's face" but could not see the complainant's hands because of the counter. A phone video taken by a customer begins just after the punch and shows the complainant on the ground and Ryan stepping back with open hands.

Ryan has no criminal record. The complainant has a pending charge for threatening a parking attendant.

The prosecution argues that the defendant attacked someone who was only arguing and that defending another person requires a real threat. The defense argues that the defendant reasonably believed the friend was about to be hit.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 42, a real estate agent, is charged with assault after a former business partner was attacked in a parking garage. The complainant suffered a broken arm.

The complainant testified to recognizing Brett clearly in the garage lights, from about two meters away, and to being hit with a metal pipe. The two had run a small property management business together until it closed eight months earlier, and the complainant was suing Brett over unpaid debts. The garage cameras were not recording that night due to a power issue.

A parking attendant saw a person in a gray rain jacket leave the garage on foot right after the attack but did not see the face. Brett owns a gray rain jacket, a very common item. No pipe was recovered.

Brett testified that he was at home alone watching television and denies any involvement. His phone shows no activity between 8:00 p.m. and 10:30 p.m.; the attack happened at 9:20 p.m. Brett's home is about 20 minutes from the garage.

The prosecution argues that the complainant knows the defendant well and could not be mistaken. The defense argues that the complainant has a financial motive to blame the defendant and that nothing else ties him to the garage.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 24, a college student who works part-time at a grocery store, is charged with assault after a house party. The complainant was found in the backyard with bruises on the face and a cracked rib.

At the hospital, the complainant told officers that "the person in the green shirt" pushed them down the back steps and kicked them. Brett was wearing a green shirt that night. At least two other guests also wore green, according to party photos. At trial, the complainant said Brett punched them before the fall, a detail not in the first statement. The complainant's blood alcohol level was 0.19.

Another guest testified to seeing Brett and the complainant arguing on the porch about ten minutes earlier. Brett admits the argument, about a borrowed speaker, but says he went back inside and left the party soon after. A ride-share receipt shows Brett was picked up 25 minutes before a guest called 911. No one saw the fall.

The prosecution argues that the defendant had a motive, matched the description, and argued with the complainant shortly before the attack. The defense argues that the description fits several guests and that the complainant's account is unreliable.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 33, an insurance agent, is charged with retail theft after leaving a home improvement store with merchandise worth $612 that had not been paid for.

Jake used a self-checkout station to buy 14 items. The receipt shows payment for 11 items totaling $96. The three unpaid items were a cordless drill, a battery pack, and a set of drill bits, which were the most expensive items in the cart. A loss prevention officer watched the transaction on camera and stopped Jake past the exit doors.

The store's own maintenance log shows that this self-checkout station had 23 recorded scanning errors in the previous month, including items that beeped but did not register. The video shows Jake passing the drill over the scanner, but the screen is not visible in the recording. The officer testified that Jake "did not look at the screen once" and moved quickly.

When stopped, Jake immediately offered to pay and showed a banking app with enough funds. He has no criminal record. The prosecution notes that the three missed items were the three most expensive ones, which it argues is unlikely to be chance.

The prosecution argues that the pattern of missed items shows intent. The defense argues that the machine was known to be faulty and that the defendant's reaction shows an honest mistake.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 28, a bartender, is charged with retail theft for taking two pairs of wireless headphones worth $698 from an electronics store.

Security video shows a person in a gray baseball cap and dark jacket placing the headphones inside a backpack and leaving without paying at 4:12 p.m. The video is low resolution, and the face is partly hidden by the cap. Twenty minutes earlier, the same person bought a phone charger at the register and scanned a loyalty card registered to Brett. The cashier could not describe the customer.

Police showed the video to Brett's former coworker, who said the person "could be" Brett because of the way they walk. No headphones were found during a search of Brett's apartment. Brett owns a gray baseball cap.

Brett testified that he often lets friends use his loyalty card number for discounts and that he was at work at the time. The bar's timekeeping system shows him clocking in at 4:45 p.m.; the bar is about 25 minutes from the store. No coworker could confirm when Brett actually arrived.

The prosecution argues that the loyalty card, the matching cap, and the coworker's statement identify the defendant. The defense argues that none of this evidence shows the face and that the card was shared.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 40, a high school teacher, is charged with retail theft of merchandise worth over $500 from a department store.

A store detective saw Brett remove the security tags from two winter coats in a fitting room and leave the store wearing one coat and carrying the other in a shopping bag. Brett was stopped outside with both coats. The ticket price on each coat was $265, for a total of $530.

The store was holding a sale that weekend, and signs on the coat rack advertised "30% off all outerwear." At the sale price, the total would have been $371. The store manager testified that the company always values stolen goods at the ticket price. The prosecution relies on that ticket value.

Brett does not deny leaving with the coats. He testified that he meant to pay at a register on another floor and forgot because he was on a phone call. The fitting room attendant testified that Brett spent about 15 minutes in the fitting room and seemed calm. The removed tags were found in a fitting room trash can. Brett had $40 in cash and two credit cards with available credit.

The prosecution argues that removing security tags shows intent and that the ticket value applies. The defense argues that intent was not proven and that the merchandise was worth less than $500 on that day.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 23, a part-time grocery store clerk, is charged with retail theft of vitamins and electric toothbrushes worth $544 from a drugstore.

Jake entered the store with an acquaintance. A camera shows the two walking together through the health products aisle, where the acquaintance's back blocks the view of the shelves for about 40 seconds. After the alarm sounded at the exit, a store employee found the merchandise in a tote bag carried by Jake. The acquaintance ran away and was never charged.

Jake testified that he did not know the items were in his bag and that the acquaintance had asked to "put something" in it while he was looking at his phone. The tote bag was open at the top. The employee testified that Jake looked "surprised" when the alarm went off but then said, "Please don't call the police."

The acquaintance has two prior shoplifting convictions and could not be found to testify. Jake has a prior juvenile record for vandalism that the jury was told about only to judge credibility.

The prosecution argues that the goods were in the defendant's bag and that the defendant asked the employee not to call the police. The defense argues that the acquaintance planted the items and that the defendant's reaction was fear, not guilt.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 35, a real estate agent, is charged with retail theft for taking four smart home cameras worth $760 from a big-box store.

Store video shows a person in a gray rain jacket and sunglasses taking the cameras from a shelf and leaving through the garden center exit without paying. The face is not clearly visible. Two days later, four cameras of the same model, still sealed, were listed for sale on an online marketplace. The listing account was created with Jake's email address, and the listing photos were taken on a kitchen counter that matches the one in Jake's apartment.

Records from the marketplace show the account was accessed from two different phones, one of which belongs to Jake. The other phone was never identified. Jake testified that his email account had been hacked months earlier and that he had reported the hack to the email provider; the provider's records confirm a report but cannot confirm the hack. Jake admits owning a gray rain jacket.

Jake has sublet a room in the apartment to short-term guests several times in the past year. No cameras were found in the apartment.

The prosecution argues that the listing, the kitchen counter, and the jacket point to the defendant. The defense argues that other people had access to the apartment and the account.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 30, a pharmacist, is charged with retail theft for taking three bottles of premium wine worth $540 from a supermarket.

A loss prevention officer testified to watching Ryan put the three bottles into a large shoulder bag in the wine aisle. Thirty minutes later, staff found the three bottles behind a planter just outside the side door.

Ryan testified that he changed his mind about buying the wine and left the bottles on a shelf in the hallway, and that someone else must have carried them outside. The officer testified that there was no shelf in the hallway.

The prosecution argues that the defendant carried the bottles out through the side door to collect them later. The defense argues that no one saw the defendant leave the store with any merchandise.

The defendant, Jake Williams, 27, a call center representative, is charged with retail theft for a return scheme at a sporting goods store. Phone records show several calls between Jake and an unregistered number that morning.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 22, a university student, is charged with retail theft of sunglasses worth $585 from a boutique in a shopping mall.

A sales associate testified to seeing a customer in a green jacket slip four pairs of designer sunglasses into a coat pocket while the associate was helping another customer. The customer left with a group of four people. The associate alerted mall security, who found the group about five minutes later in the food court. Ryan was the only person in the group wearing a green jacket. The four pairs of sunglasses were found in a trash can about ten meters from the table where the group was sitting.

The associate later identified Ryan as the person in the green jacket, but admitted that two other customers in the store that afternoon also wore green. The boutique camera was not recording because of a system update. No sunglasses were found on any member of the group.

Ryan testified that he was in the boutique only briefly and never touched the sunglasses. The other three members of the group testified that they did not see anyone take anything. The prosecution notes that they are close friends of Ryan.

The prosecution argues that the associate's account, the green jacket, and the nearby trash can establish guilt. The defense argues that the identification relies only on clothing and that anyone in the food court could have discarded the sunglasses.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 32, an insurance appraiser, is charged with residential burglary of a detached house. While the owners were away for a weekend, someone forced open a rear window and took jewelry, a laptop, and about $800 in cash.

Investigators lifted two fingerprints from the outside of the forced window frame. Both matched Ryan. Fresh pry marks on the frame matched a flat screwdriver, a common tool. About five weeks earlier, Ryan had inspected storm damage to the rear windows of the house for the owners' insurance company, as the claim file confirms.

The owners testified that they washed the outside of the windows "sometime in the past month" but could not say exactly when. A fingerprint expert testified that prints on a painted window frame can last for weeks if not cleaned, and that the age of a print cannot be determined.

Ryan testified that he spent the weekend at home. His roommate confirmed that Ryan was home Saturday evening, but was away Sunday afternoon, when the neighbors believe the burglary happened because a dog barked for a long time. None of the stolen items were found during a search of Ryan's apartment and car.

The prosecution argues that the prints were on the exact window that was forced. The defense argues that the prints are explained by the insurance inspection and that nothing else links the defendant to the burglary.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 29, a restaurant shift manager, is charged with residential burglary of an apartment from which a gold watch, two rings, and a tablet were taken.

Two days after the burglary, Jake sold the gold watch to a pawn shop, showing his own driver's license and signing the receipt. The watch had a unique engraving that the owner described before it was recovered. The other items were never found.

Jake testified that he bought the watch for $150 from a stranger at a gas station, believing it was a good deal, and sold it to the pawn shop for $400 the same week. He could not give the stranger's name or a clear description. The gas station's cameras keep footage for only 24 hours.

There were no fingerprints, shoe prints, or DNA linking Jake to the apartment. Jake's phone was not near the apartment on the day of the burglary, according to cell tower records. The watch's market value is about $1,200. A detective testified that buying a watch for far less than its value is "a classic sign" of knowing it was stolen, which would be a different crime than burglary.

The prosecution argues that possession of recently stolen property, with a weak explanation, supports the inference that the defendant committed the burglary. The defense argues that the evidence shows, at most, that the defendant bought stolen property, not that he entered the apartment.

Latonya testified that she bought the watch for $150 from a stranger at a gas station, believing it was a good deal, and sold it to the pawn shop for $400 the same week. She could not give the stranger's name or a clear description. The gas station's cameras keep footage for only 24 hours.

There were no fingerprints, shoe prints, or DNA linking Latonya to the apartment. Latonya's phone was not near the apartment on the day of the burglary, according to cell tower records. The watch's market value is about $1,200. A detective testified that buying a watch for far less than its value is "a classic sign" of knowing it was stolen, which would be a different crime than burglary.

The prosecution argues that possession of recently stolen property, with a weak explanation, supports the inference that the defendant committed the burglary. The defense argues that the evidence shows, at most, that the defendant bought stolen property, not that she entered the apartment.

The defendant, Jake Williams, 25, a junior accountant, is charged with residential burglary of a townhouse. Someone kicked in the back door on a weekday morning and took two laptops and a gaming console.

Investigators photographed a muddy shoe print on the kitchen floor. The print matches the sole pattern and size of a running shoe found in Jake's closet. A shoe expert testified that the model is one of the best-selling running shoes in the country and that the print showed no unique wear marks that would tie it to a specific pair.

Cell tower data places Jake's phone in the area of the townhouse between 9:00 and 11:30 a.m. Jake's close friend lives about four blocks away, and the friend testified that Jake came over that morning to help move furniture and stayed "most of the morning," but could not say whether Jake left for any period.

A neighbor saw a person in a dark hooded jacket carrying a large bag near the townhouse at about 10:15 a.m. but could not describe the face. Jake owns a dark hooded jacket. None of the stolen items were found.

The prosecution argues that the shoe print, the phone location, and the jacket together point to the defendant. The defense argues that each piece of evidence is common and that the defendant had an innocent reason to be in the area.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 38, a sales representative, is charged with residential burglary of a house. Someone broke a glass panel in the back door and stole a coin collection worth about $9,000.

A cigarette butt found on the back patio, about two meters from the broken door, contained Brett's DNA. Brett lived in the house next door until three months before the burglary and was friendly with the homeowners. The homeowners testified that Brett sometimes smoked on their patio during backyard gatherings, and that they could not remember when they last swept the patio.

The homeowners had shown the coin collection to several visitors over the years, including Brett. A neighbor's camera recorded a car similar to Brett's, a common silver sedan, passing on the street 40 minutes before the estimated time of the burglary. The plate is not readable.

Brett testified that he was at his new apartment that evening. He has no witnesses. Bank records show that Brett had fallen behind on rent and had received a late notice the week before. No coins were found, and no coin dealer in the region reported buying the collection.

The prosecution argues that the DNA, the knowledge of the collection, the car, and the financial pressure point to the defendant. The defense argues that the DNA could be months old and that the car and motive are speculation.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 27, a graphic designer, is charged with residential burglary of an apartment he used to share with the complainant. Three months after Ryan moved out, someone entered the apartment while it was empty and took a camera, two lenses, and an envelope with $1,500 in cash.

There was no forced entry. Ryan admits never returning his key. The complainant testified that two other people also had keys: a dog walker and a former partner of the complainant. Both testified that they did not enter the apartment that day and gave alibis that were partly confirmed.

The complainant testified that Ryan knew where the cash envelope was kept, because the two used to share a household budget. A text message from Ryan sent two weeks before the burglary says, "You still owe me for the last two months of utilities, and I'm going to get it one way or another." Ryan testified that the message was about filing a small claims case.

Ryan says he was at a coworking space that afternoon. The coworking space logs show his badge entering at 1:10 p.m. and no exit record, because exits are not logged. The apartment is a 20-minute walk from the coworking space. None of the stolen items were found.

The prosecution argues that the key, the knowledge of the cash, and the threatening message point to the defendant. The defense argues that others had keys and that the message referred to a lawful claim.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 34, a hospital pharmacist who works night shifts, is charged with residential burglary after being found at about 3:30 a.m. inside the attached garage of a house two blocks from his own home. Under state law, an attached garage is part of the dwelling.

The homeowner heard noises, looked out, and saw a person with a flashlight open the side door of the garage and step inside. The homeowner called 911. Police arrived within six minutes and found Ryan inside the garage, wearing gloves and holding a flashlight, standing next to a shelf with power tools. Nothing was missing.

Ryan testified that his cat had escaped that evening and that he was searching nearby yards after getting home from work. He said he heard a noise inside the garage, found the side door unlocked, and stepped in to look for the cat. A neighbor confirmed seeing a "lost cat" post from Ryan on a local community app at 1:50 a.m. The cat was found two days later, three streets away.

The homeowner testified that the side door was locked earlier that night. Police did not test the handle for prints. Ryan wears gloves on the way home from work in cold weather; the temperature that night was 2°C.

The prosecution argues that the defendant entered the garage with the intent to steal the tools. The defense argues that the defendant entered only to look for a lost pet, without any intent to commit a theft.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 26, a barista, is charged with residential burglary of a house from which a laptop, a tablet, and a set of headphones were stolen during the day.

The laptop had tracking software. Two days after the burglary, the owner located it at a house where Ryan rents a room with three other tenants. Police found the laptop in a shared living room, plugged in, with the owner's account still logged in. The tablet and headphones were not found.

One of the other tenants had moved out the day after the burglary and could not be located. Ryan testified that this tenant brought the laptop home and said it had been "bought cheap from a friend." The remaining two tenants testified that they had never seen the laptop before, but also said they rarely used the living room.

A neighbor of the burglarized house saw a person on a bicycle leave the house carrying a backpack. Ryan owns a bicycle, as do the other tenants. Phone location data places Ryan at work during most of the estimated burglary window, but there is a 50-minute gap during his lunch break; the house is about 10 minutes away by bicycle.

The prosecution argues that the defendant had the stolen laptop and the opportunity to commit the burglary during the lunch break. The defense argues that the laptop was in a shared space and was brought in by a tenant who then disappeared.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 31, a postal mail carrier, is charged with residential burglary of a house on his delivery route. Someone entered through an unlocked back door during the day and took a tablet, a laptop, and several pieces of jewelry.

A neighbor testified to seeing Brett, whom the neighbor recognized as the regular mail carrier, walking along the side of the house toward the backyard at about 2:00 p.m. Postal scan records show that Brett delivered a package to that house at 1:57 p.m. The package was left at the front door.

The homeowners left for work at 8:00 a.m. and returned at 6:30 p.m., so the burglary could have happened at any time during that period. A different neighbor saw a person in a gray sweatshirt in the backyard "sometime in the afternoon" but could not describe the face.

Brett testified that he walked toward the side gate only to check whether there was a safer place to leave the package, as he sometimes does, and then left it at the front door. His postal vehicle's GPS shows him at the next stop four minutes later. None of the stolen items were found in his vehicle or home.

The prosecution argues that the defendant was seen going toward the back of the house shortly before the items went missing. The defense argues that four minutes was not enough time and that the burglary window was ten hours long.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 36, a freelance photographer, is charged with residential burglary of a house where a glass patio door was smashed and electronics worth about $4,000 were taken.

Police stopped Jake about one kilometer from the house, 50 minutes after a neighbor reported the sound of breaking glass. A lab analysis found three tiny glass fragments on Jake's jacket with the same refractive index as the patio door glass. A glass expert testified that this type of glass is used in millions of doors and windows and that the match shows only that the fragments could have come from the door. Blue fibers found on the broken door frame were consistent with Jake's jacket, a mass-produced item.

Jake testified that he spent the evening at a friend's home helping repair a broken window, which explains the glass. The friend confirmed this and showed a receipt for window glass bought that afternoon, but the friend's broken window used a different type of glass, according to the expert.

No stolen items were found on Jake or in his car. Jake has a conviction for burglary from 11 years ago.

The prosecution argues that the glass and fiber evidence, together with the stop near the scene, identify the defendant. The defense argues that the forensic matches are generic and that the defendant has a credible reason for having glass on the jacket.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 39, a staff accountant, is charged with embezzlement from the furniture company where he worked. Over seven months, 14 payments totaling $48,300 were sent from the company's bank account to a vendor that does not exist. The vendor's bank account was opened online with a stolen identity.

All 14 payments were approved in the accounting system under Ryan's login. Ryan was one of three people in the accounting office, and the office shared one computer for bank approvals. Two coworkers testified that Ryan's password was written on a sticky note attached to that computer's monitor, a practice the company's auditors had criticized.

Four of the payments were approved on days when Ryan was working from home, according to the badge system; the company's remote access logs show Ryan's account connected from his home internet address on those days. The other two employees' accounts do not show remote access on those days.

Ryan testified that he never approved those payments and that anyone in the office could have used his login. Investigators found no unusual deposits in Ryan's bank accounts. He had taken on a large personal loan the year before.

The prosecution argues that the login records and remote access link the defendant to the payments. The defense argues that the password was public in the office and that no money was traced to the defendant.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 44, an office operations manager, is charged with embezzlement from a small architecture firm. Over two years, Ryan deposited 22 company checks, totaling $36,750, into his personal bank account.

Ryan admits making the deposits. He testified that one of the firm's two founding partners verbally authorized the checks as reimbursement for expenses he paid personally, including software licenses and client dinners, and as an informal bonus. That partner died of a heart attack eight months before the trial. The surviving partner testified to knowing nothing about any reimbursement agreement and said that the firm's written policy requires receipts for every reimbursement.

Ryan produced receipts for about $9,400 in business expenses paid with his own card during the same period. The memo lines on several checks say "reimb." in Ryan's handwriting. Two of the checks bear the deceased partner's signature; the others were signed with a signature stamp that Ryan was allowed to use for routine bills.

The firm's bookkeeper testified that the deceased partner "was informal about money" and sometimes gave cash bonuses without recording them.

The prosecution argues that the defendant used the signature stamp to pay himself far more than any documented expense. The defense argues that the payments were authorized by a partner who can no longer testify.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 26, a shift supervisor at a gas station convenience store, is charged with embezzlement of about $6,200 in cash over three months.

His bank records show regular cash deposits of $100 to $200 during the period, which he says come from weekend work as a wedding photographer's assistant; he produced two payment messages from the photographer.

The prosecution argues that the pattern of shortages and the access to the safe point to the defendant. The defense argues that others had access and that shortages continued after the suspension.

The defendant, Jake Williams, 35, an accounting systems analyst responsible for payroll processing, is charged with embezzlement from a regional trucking company. For 15 months, a person who never worked at the company received biweekly paychecks totaling $41,600. The paychecks were deposited into an account controlled by the company's operations manager.

Jake created the fake employee record in the payroll system and approved each pay run. Jake admits creating the record but testified that the operations manager told him the person was a remote dispatcher hired off the books and that he should "just put them in the system." Emails show the operations manager sending Jake the fake employee's name, address, and bank details.

The operations manager was also charged and agreed to testify against Jake in exchange for a reduced sentence. The manager testified that Jake came up with the scheme and received $500 in cash from each paycheck. No cash payments to Jake were traced. Jake's bank account shows no unusual deposits, but he bought a used car with $7,000 in cash during the period; he testified that the money came from savings.

Company policy required payroll staff to verify any new employee with a signed hiring form. No form exists for the fake employee.

The prosecution argues that the defendant knowingly created and paid a fake employee and shared in the proceeds. The defense argues that the defendant followed a manager's instructions and that the manager is lying to reduce a sentence.

The defendant, Jake Williams, 24, a customer service desk associate at a department store, is charged with embezzlement for processing refunds onto his own debit card. Over four months, 31 refunds totaling $5,860 were paid to a card in Jake's name. No returned merchandise matches most of those refunds.

Jake admits that the refunds went to his card. He testified that, on busy days, some customers who paid in cash wanted their refunds immediately, and that he refunded those amounts to his own card and handed the customers cash from his wallet, because the store's cash refund process took too long. He said a former supervisor told him this was acceptable.

The former supervisor denies giving that permission. The store found returned merchandise logged for 6 of the 31 refunds. For the other 25, there is no record of returned items. Store video for three of those refunds shows no customer at the desk at the time.

Jake withdrew cash from ATMs on most of the days the refunds were processed, which the defense says is consistent with replacing the cash he gave to customers. Jake has been employed at the store for three years with no prior discipline.

The prosecution argues that refunds without customers and without merchandise show theft. The defense argues that the defendant used an informal, unauthorized but honest workaround.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 31, an inventory analyst at an electronics distributor, is charged with embezzlement of company inventory. Over six months, 46 new graphics cards worth $27,000 disappeared from the warehouse, and inventory records were adjusted to hide the losses.

The prosecution argues that the defendant hid the losses so the housemate could sell the stolen cards and shared in the profits. The defense argues that the defendant did his job and reported the shortages, and that the housemate acted alone.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 37, a treasury analyst at a community credit union, is charged with embezzlement of $52,000. Investigators found that, over two years, small amounts were moved from dormant member accounts into an internal suspense account and then transferred to an outside account belonging to a company registered under a false name.

A spreadsheet tracking the dormant accounts and the transfers was found on Ryan's work computer. The transfers were made with two different employee logins, Ryan's and that of a coworker who left the credit union a year earlier and could not be found.

After a three-hour meeting with the board and the credit union's lawyer, Ryan wrote an email to the board: "I should have reported what was happening with the dormant accounts. Ryan testified that his "part" was failing to report suspicious transfers he had noticed, not making them, and that the spreadsheet was his own effort to track the problem.

The outside company's bank account was opened with a phone number that once belonged to the former coworker. No money was traced to Ryan.

The prosecution argues that the spreadsheet, the login records, and the email admission show guilt. The defense argues that the defendant was investigating, not committing, the scheme and that the former coworker is the likely culprit.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 29, a pharmacy manager, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a cyclist at about 11:20 p.m. on a two-lane road. The cyclist suffered a broken leg. A witness wrote down a partial plate and described a silver hatchback.

Police found Ryan's silver hatchback the next morning with a cracked headlight and a dent on the front right fender. Paint transfer from the bicycle matched the dent. The plate matches the witness's partial plate.

Ryan shares the car with his housemate, and both have keys. Ryan testified that he was asleep at home that night and that the housemate had borrowed the car to visit friends. The housemate testified to returning the car at 9:30 p.m., before the collision, and to being at home after that. Neither person's phone shows movement after 10:00 p.m., but the prosecution notes that the driver may not have carried a phone.

The witness saw the driver only from behind and could not describe the person. No camera recorded the driver. The car's seat position fit both Ryan and the housemate.

The prosecution argues that the defendant's car was involved and that the defendant, as the owner and primary user, was most likely the driver. The defense argues that two people had access to the car and that the prosecution cannot prove who was driving.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 52, a high school chemistry teacher, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian at about 6:40 p.m. on a rainy winter evening. The pedestrian was walking in the road at the edge of a narrow street without sidewalks, was struck by a side mirror, and fell into a ditch, suffering a broken wrist and a concussion.

Jake admits driving on that street at the time and admits feeling "a bump." He testified that he thought he had hit a pothole, which is common on that street, and kept driving home. The next morning, Jake noticed that the right side mirror was broken and reported it to his insurer as pothole damage.

A neighbor who heard the impact testified that it was "a loud bang" and that the car did not slow down. The pedestrian was wearing dark clothing and no reflective gear. An accident reconstruction expert testified that a driver could have seen the pedestrian in the headlights for about two seconds before impact, but that after impact the pedestrian fell to the right, outside the driver's line of sight.

The street has several deep potholes, which the city had been asked to repair. Jake has a clean driving record.

The prosecution argues that a loud impact and a broken mirror should have made any reasonable driver stop and check. The defense argues that the defendant honestly believed he hit a pothole and did not know a person was involved.

Ryan testified that the other driver said "don't worry about it" and did not appear hurt. The other driver denies saying that. Ryan contacted the supermarket the next day asking whether anyone had reported damage, which the store manager confirmed.

The prosecution argues that the defendant left without exchanging information after a collision that caused injury. The defense argues that the defendant stopped, checked, believed no one was hurt, and later tried to follow up.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 25, a graduate student, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian outside a concert venue at about 11:55 p.m. The pedestrian suffered a head injury.

Several people saw Ryan's car pull out of a parking spot quickly and saw the pedestrian fall in the street near the car. Ryan drove away. A breath test taken three hours later, when police found Ryan at home, showed a blood alcohol level of 0.05; an expert estimated that it was about 0.09 at the time of the incident.

The pedestrian, who had also been drinking, remembers nothing. Two witnesses said they saw the car's bumper hit the pedestrian. A third witness said the pedestrian stepped off the curb, tripped, and fell next to the car without being hit. A forensic examination found no damage, fibers, or biological traces on Ryan's car. The emergency physician testified that the injury is consistent with a fall from standing height, with or without being struck.

Ryan testified that he saw someone fall near the car, thought the person had tripped, and left because he was afraid of being caught driving after drinking.

The prosecution argues that witnesses saw the impact and that fleeing shows the defendant knew there was a collision. The defense argues that the forensic evidence does not show any impact and that fear of a drinking charge explains the departure.
